about: Foundations of Evidence-Based Practice (FEBP) is a first-year 2nd MB subject for Cambridge medical (and veterinary) students. It introduces epidemiology and biostatistics so that students become informed consumers of research. It is taught through ten lectures across Michaelmas and Lent terms (introduction to EBP, using knowledge, generating knowledge, ruling out chance, comparing groups, using study results, beyond single studies, diagnosis and screening, then academia and review) plus four seminars discussing published papers. It is assessed by a single 45-minute multiple-choice paper at the end of Lent term. The topics below follow the official learning outcomes, in the order of the lecture sequence; the lecture titles are broad, so matching outcomes to lectures is our own.
topics: Evidence-based practice and the focused clinical question
Ruling out chance: p values and confidence intervals
Comparing groups: choosing a hypothesis test
Using study results: 2×2 tables, risks and odds
Beyond single studies: systematic reviews and meta-analysis

notes.h: Evidence-based practice and asking a focused question
notes.body:
Evidence-based practice (EBP) is the idea that clinical decisions should rest on the best available research, not just habit or authority. The classic definition comes from David Sackett and colleagues (BMJ, 1996): evidence-based medicine is the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients.

Three things are combined:
- the best available research evidence
- the clinician's expertise and judgement
- the patient's values, preferences and circumstances

EBP is not "cookbook medicine". Evidence from trials describes average effects in selected groups; the clinician still has to judge whether it applies to the patient in front of them.

The five steps (the "5 As")
- Ask a focused, answerable question.
- Acquire the evidence by searching the literature.
- Appraise it for validity, size of effect and relevance.
- Apply it, together with expertise and the patient's preferences.
- Assess (audit) the outcome and your own performance.

Framing the question: PICO
- P: patient or population (who?)
- I: intervention or exposure (what is being done or what are they exposed to?)
- C: comparison (placebo, usual care, another drug, no exposure)
- O: outcome (what matters, ideally a patient-important outcome such as death or stroke rather than a surrogate such as a blood test)
Example: "In adults with type 2 diabetes (P), does drug X (I) compared with standard care (C) reduce cardiovascular death (O)?" Variants add T (time) or S (study design).

Searching the literature
- Main databases: MEDLINE (searched free through PubMed), Embase, and the Cochrane Library for systematic reviews and trials.
- Combine terms with Boolean operators: OR widens (synonyms), AND narrows (combining PICO elements), NOT excludes.
- Use controlled vocabulary such as MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) as well as free-text words, truncation (e.g. diabet*) and filters for study type.

Matching the design to the question
- Therapy or prevention: randomised controlled trial (RCT), or a systematic review of RCTs.
- Harm or aetiology: cohort or case-control study (an RCT of a harmful exposure would be unethical).
- Prognosis: cohort study.
- Diagnosis: cross-sectional comparison of a test against a reference standard.
- Experience and meaning: qualitative methods such as interviews and focus groups.

The "hierarchy of evidence" (systematic reviews and RCTs at the top, then cohort, case-control, case series, and expert opinion at the bottom) is a useful rough guide for questions about treatment, but it is not absolute: a well-conducted cohort study can be more informative than a small, biased trial.

Research beyond the lecture theatre
The course also wants you to see how knowledge is produced: research questions lead to protocols, ethics approval, data collection and outputs such as conference abstracts, posters and peer-reviewed papers. As a student you can get involved through projects, audits and intercalated research.

Exam tips: be able to turn a clinical scenario into a PICO question, and to name the study design best suited to a therapy, harm, prognosis or diagnosis question.

Study designs fall into two broad groups: observational (the researcher measures but does not assign exposure) and interventional or experimental (the researcher assigns the intervention).

Descriptive observational designs
- Case report or case series: describes one or a few patients. Good for spotting new diseases or rare side effects; no comparison group, so cannot test causation.
- Cross-sectional study (survey): measures exposure and outcome at one point in time. Gives prevalence. Cannot show which came first (temporality).
- Ecological study: compares groups or populations (e.g. countries), not individuals. Risk of the ecological fallacy: assuming a group-level association holds for individuals.

Analytical observational designs
- Case-control study: start with people who have the disease (cases) and people who do not (controls), then look back at past exposure.
  - Strengths: quick and cheap; good for rare diseases and diseases with long latency; can study many exposures.
  - Weaknesses: recall bias, difficulty choosing appropriate controls (selection bias); cannot measure incidence, so the measure of effect is the odds ratio.
  - Example: Doll and Hill's 1950 BMJ study comparing smoking in lung cancer patients and controls.
- Cohort study: start with people free of the outcome, classify by exposure, follow them up to see who develops the outcome. Can be prospective or retrospective (historical, using existing records).
  - Strengths: establishes temporality; measures incidence, so gives relative risk; good for rare exposures; can study several outcomes.
  - Weaknesses: slow and expensive; loss to follow-up; inefficient for rare outcomes; still open to confounding.
  - Example: the British Doctors Study, which followed doctors from 1951 and linked smoking to deaths from lung cancer and other causes.

Interventional design: the randomised controlled trial (RCT)
- Participants are randomly allocated to intervention or control. Randomisation, if large enough, balances known and unknown confounders between groups, which is why RCTs are the best design for testing treatments.
- Allocation concealment: whoever enrols participants must not know the next allocation, otherwise selection bias creeps back in.
- Blinding (masking) of participants, clinicians and outcome assessors reduces performance and detection bias. "Double-blind" usually means participants and investigators are blinded.
- Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis analyses everyone in the group to which they were randomised, preserving the benefits of randomisation; per-protocol analysis includes only those who followed the protocol and can be biased.
- Variants: crossover trials (each participant receives both treatments in sequence, suits stable chronic conditions), cluster trials (randomise groups such as GP practices), factorial trials (test two interventions at once).
- Limitations: expensive, may use selected participants (limiting generalisability, or external validity), and may be unethical for harmful exposures.

Internal validity means the result is correct for the people studied (free from bias and confounding); external validity means it can be generalised to other people and settings.

Exam tips: in MCQs, look for the direction of time (outcome first means case-control; exposure first means cohort) and remember which measure each design yields: prevalence (cross-sectional), odds ratio (case-control), relative risk (cohort and RCT).

Research almost always studies a sample and uses it to make inferences about a wider population. How the sample is chosen and how the data are summarised are basic skills tested in FEBP.

Sampling
- Target population: the people we want to draw conclusions about. Sampling frame: the list from which the sample is actually drawn (e.g. a GP register).
- Probability sampling (every member has a known chance of selection):
  - simple random sampling
  - systematic sampling (every kth person on a list)
  - stratified sampling (random sampling within subgroups such as age bands, so each is represented)
  - cluster sampling (randomly choose groups such as schools, then study people within them; cheaper but less precise)
- Non-probability sampling: convenience, purposive (common in qualitative research), snowball (useful for hard-to-reach groups) and quota sampling. Cheaper but more prone to selection bias.
- Sampling error is the chance difference between a sample and the population; it shrinks as sample size increases. Bias is systematic and does not shrink with a bigger sample.

Types of data
- Categorical: nominal (no order, e.g. blood group) or ordinal (ordered, e.g. pain mild/moderate/severe, cancer stage).
- Numerical: discrete (counts, e.g. number of admissions) or continuous (e.g. blood pressure, weight).
The type of data decides how you summarise it and which statistical test you use.

Summarising numerical data
- Central tendency: mean (sum divided by n), median (middle value), mode (most common value).
- Spread: range, interquartile range (IQR, from the 25th to the 75th centile), variance and standard deviation (SD).
- For roughly symmetrical (Normal) data, report mean and SD. For skewed data, report median and IQR, because the mean is pulled towards the tail.
- In right (positive) skew, the tail is to the right and mean > median; in left (negative) skew, mean < median.

Worked example: values 2, 4, 4, 5, 10.
- Mean = 25/5 = 5; median = 4; mode = 4.
- Deviations from the mean: −3, −1, −1, 0, 5; squared: 9, 1, 1, 0, 25; sum = 36.
- Sample variance = 36/(n − 1) = 36/4 = 9, so SD = 3.
- The single high value (10) pulls the mean above the median: right skew.

The Normal distribution
- Symmetrical and bell-shaped, described by its mean and SD.
- About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 1.96 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD.
- A "normal range" (reference range) for a lab test is often defined as mean ± 1.96 SD, so 5% of healthy people fall outside it by definition.

Standard deviation versus standard error
- SD describes the spread of individual observations.
- Standard error of the mean (SE) = SD/√n describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean. It falls as n rises. Quadrupling the sample size halves the SE.

Exam tips: never confuse SD with SE, and check whether data are skewed before deciding whether mean or median is the right summary.

Any difference seen in a sample might be due to chance. Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals are the two standard tools for judging this.

Hypothesis testing
- Null hypothesis (H0): there is no difference or no association in the population (e.g. the new drug and placebo have the same effect).
- Alternative hypothesis (H1): there is a difference.
- The test calculates a test statistic and from it a p value.

The p value
- Definition: the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true.
- It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about how big or important the effect is.
- By convention p < 0.05 is called "statistically significant" (the significance level, α = 0.05), but this cut-off is arbitrary. Report exact p values where possible.

Errors
- Type I error: rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive). Its probability is α.
- Type II error: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative). Its probability is β.
- Power = 1 − β: the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size. Trials usually aim for 80% or 90% power.
- Power rises with larger sample size, larger true effect, less variability in the outcome and a less strict α. Small studies are often "underpowered": a non-significant result may just mean the study was too small, and absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

Multiple testing
- If you run 20 independent tests at α = 0.05 when there are no real effects, you expect about one "significant" result by chance. Pre-specify the primary outcome; corrections such as Bonferroni (divide α by the number of tests) are one remedy.

Confidence intervals (CIs)
- A 95% CI gives a range of plausible values for the true population value. Strictly: if the study were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals calculated this way would contain the true value.
- For a mean (large samples): 95% CI = estimate ± 1.96 × SE.
- Worked example: a trial finds a mean fall in systolic blood pressure of 6 mmHg more with drug than placebo, SE 2 mmHg. 95% CI = 6 ± 1.96 × 2 = 6 ± 3.92, i.e. 2.08 to 9.92 mmHg. The interval excludes 0, so the difference is statistically significant at the 5% level.
- Line of no effect: 0 for differences (in means or risks), 1 for ratios (relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio). If a 95% CI excludes the line of no effect, the two-sided p value is below 0.05; if it includes it, p is above 0.05.
- A wide CI means an imprecise estimate (usually a small study). CIs are more informative than p values because they show size and precision together.

Statistical versus clinical significance
- A very large study can find a tiny, clinically meaningless difference that is statistically significant. A small study can miss an important effect.
- Ask whether the whole CI lies within a range that would matter to patients.

Exam tips: memorise the exact wording of the p value definition, the link between CIs and the line of no effect, and the four factors that increase power.

notes.h: Comparing groups: choosing a hypothesis test
notes.body:
FEBP expects you to choose a suitable test for a given study, justify the choice and state its assumptions. You will not be asked to do long calculations by hand, but you should recognise the right test and read the output.

Questions to ask
- What type of outcome? Numerical (continuous) or categorical (e.g. alive/dead)?
- How many groups? One sample against a known value, two groups, or more than two?
- Are the groups independent (different people) or paired (the same people measured twice, or matched pairs)?
- For numerical data, is it roughly Normal (use a parametric test) or skewed/ordinal (use a non-parametric, rank-based test)?

Numerical outcome, Normal data (parametric tests)
- One-sample t-test: compares a sample mean with a fixed value.
- Paired t-test: compares two measurements on the same people (e.g. blood pressure before and after treatment); it tests whether the mean of the differences is zero.
- Independent (two-sample) t-test: compares means of two separate groups. Assumes independent observations, roughly Normal data in each group and (for the classic Student's version) similar variances; Welch's version relaxes the equal-variance assumption.
- More than two groups: one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).

Numerical or ordinal outcome, non-Normal data (non-parametric tests)
- Wilcoxon signed-rank test: paired data (non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test).
- Mann–Whitney U test (also called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test): two independent groups.
- Kruskal–Wallis test: more than two independent groups.
These make fewer assumptions but are generally less powerful when data really are Normal.

Categorical outcome
- Chi-squared (χ²) test: compares proportions between independent groups in a contingency table. Rule of thumb: expected counts should be at least 5 in most cells.
- Fisher's exact test: for 2×2 tables with small expected counts.
- McNemar's test: paired binary data (e.g. the same patients tested by two methods).

Worked chi-squared example
100 patients get treatment (30 have the event) and 100 get control (50 have the event). Overall 80/200 have the event.
- Expected events in each arm = row total × column total / grand total = 100 × 80/200 = 40; expected non-events = 60.
- χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = (30−40)²/40 + (70−60)²/60 + (50−40)²/40 + (50−60)²/60 = 2.5 + 1.67 + 2.5 + 1.67 ≈ 8.33.
- A 2×2 table has 1 degree of freedom; the 5% critical value is 3.84. Since 8.33 > 3.84, p < 0.05 and we reject the null hypothesis of no difference.

Relationships between two numerical variables
- Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) measures linear association (−1 to +1) and assumes roughly Normal data; Spearman's rank correlation is the non-parametric version.
- Correlation is not causation, and r measures strength of a linear association, not the slope.
- Linear regression estimates how much the outcome changes per unit change in the predictor; multiple regression adjusts for several variables at once (used to handle confounding).

Exam tips: build a mental table of outcome type × number of groups × paired/independent. MCQs often hinge on spotting that data are paired or skewed.

FEBP explicitly requires you to build a 2×2 table and calculate and interpret a relative risk (RR) and odds ratio (OR). Lay the table out the same way every time.

Standard layout (rows = exposure or treatment, columns = outcome)
- Exposed: a with outcome, b without
- Unexposed: c with outcome, d without

Measures
- Risk in exposed = a/(a + b); risk in unexposed = c/(c + d).
- Relative risk (risk ratio) RR = [a/(a + b)] / [c/(c + d)].
- Odds in exposed = a/b; odds in unexposed = c/d.
- Odds ratio OR = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc.
- RR or OR of 1 means no association; above 1 means the exposure increases the outcome; below 1 means it is associated with less of the outcome (e.g. a protective treatment).

Treatment effects in trials
- Control event rate (CER) and experimental event rate (EER).
- Absolute risk reduction ARR = CER − EER.
- Relative risk reduction RRR = ARR/CER = 1 − RR.
- Number needed to treat NNT = 1/ARR (round up to a whole number): the number of patients who must be treated for one extra patient to benefit. If the treatment increases harm, the equivalent is the number needed to harm (NNH = 1/absolute risk increase).

Worked example
An RCT allocates 200 patients to each arm. 20 treated patients and 40 control patients have a stroke.
- EER = 20/200 = 10%; CER = 40/200 = 20%.
- RR = 0.10/0.20 = 0.5 (treatment halves the risk).
- RRR = 50%; ARR = 20% − 10% = 10% (0.10).
- NNT = 1/0.10 = 10.
- OR = (20 × 160)/(180 × 40) = 3200/7200 ≈ 0.44.
Note that the OR (0.44) is further from 1 than the RR (0.5). The OR approximates the RR only when the outcome is rare (roughly under 10%).

Which measure for which design?
- Cohort studies and RCTs measure incidence, so they can give risks, RR, ARR and NNT.
- Case-control studies choose participants by outcome, so the proportion with the outcome is set by the researcher; risks cannot be calculated and the OR is used. Because the OR is the same whichever way the table is read, the exposure OR from a case-control study estimates the disease OR.

Absolute versus relative presentation
- Relative measures sound more impressive. A drug that cuts risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000 has an RRR of 50% but an ARR of only 0.1% (NNT 1,000).
- Patients and clinicians need absolute risks to weigh benefit against harm and cost, so good communication gives both.

Other quantities you may meet
- Hazard ratio (HR): from survival analysis; interpreted like a relative rate over time.
- Attributable risk: risk in exposed minus risk in unexposed (the excess risk due to exposure, if causal).
- Always read the CI: an RR of 0.8 with 95% CI 0.6 to 1.1 crosses 1 and is not statistically significant.

Exam tips: write the table out before calculating, check which row is "exposed", and show ARR as a proportion (0.10), not a percentage, when you take its reciprocal for NNT.

Before concluding that an exposure causes an outcome, rule out three alternative explanations: chance (covered by statistics), bias and confounding. Reverse causation is a fourth to consider.

Bias: systematic error that pushes results away from the truth. A bigger sample does not fix it.
- Selection bias: the people studied differ systematically from the target population, or comparison groups differ in how they were selected or retained. Examples: volunteers tend to be healthier; the healthy worker effect (employed people are healthier than the general population); differential loss to follow-up; poor choice of controls in a case-control study.
- Information (measurement) bias: exposure or outcome is measured inaccurately or differently between groups.
  - Recall bias: cases may remember past exposures more thoroughly than controls (a classic problem in case-control studies).
  - Observer or interviewer bias: assessors who know a participant's group may record outcomes differently (reduced by blinding).
  - Misclassification can be non-differential (similar in both groups, usually biases towards no effect) or differential (unpredictable direction).
- Publication bias: positive studies are more likely to be published (see systematic reviews).

Confounding
A confounder is a third variable that:
- is associated with the exposure,
- is an independent cause (or risk factor) of the outcome, and
- is not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.
Example: an observed association between coffee drinking and lung cancer could be confounded by smoking, because smokers drink more coffee and smoking causes lung cancer.

Controlling confounding
- At the design stage: randomisation (balances known and unknown confounders), restriction (e.g. study only non-smokers), matching (e.g. controls matched to cases by age and sex).
- At the analysis stage: stratification (analyse within levels of the confounder, e.g. Mantel–Haenszel methods) and multivariable regression ("adjusted" estimates).
- Observational studies can only adjust for confounders that were measured, and measured accurately; residual confounding is always possible. This is why RCTs are preferred for questions about treatment.

Effect modification is different: the size of an effect genuinely varies across subgroups (e.g. a drug works better in women than men). It is a real finding to report, not a nuisance to remove.

Reverse causation: the outcome causes the exposure. For example, people may stop drinking alcohol because they are ill, making non-drinkers look less healthy. Designs that establish temporality (cohorts, trials) help.

Assessing causality: the Bradford Hill viewpoints
In 1965 Sir Austin Bradford Hill set out nine considerations for judging whether an association is causal:
- strength of association
- consistency (repeated in different studies and settings)
- specificity
- temporality (cause before effect)
- biological gradient (dose-response)
- plausibility
- coherence with existing knowledge
- experiment (e.g. removing the exposure reduces the outcome)
- analogy
Hill presented these as aids to judgement, not a checklist. Only temporality is essential: the cause must come before the effect.

Exam tips: when an MCQ describes an association, name the specific bias or confounder that could explain it and say how the design could have prevented it.

A single study can be wrong through chance or bias, and different studies of the same question often disagree. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses bring the evidence together.

Narrative versus systematic reviews
- A narrative (traditional) review summarises literature chosen by the author; it can be selective and biased.
- A systematic review uses a pre-specified, reproducible method to find, appraise and combine all relevant studies on a focused question.

Steps in a systematic review
- A focused question (often in PICO form) and a written protocol, ideally registered in advance (e.g. on PROSPERO), so methods cannot be changed after seeing the results.
- A comprehensive search of several databases plus trial registers, reference lists and grey literature (unpublished material) to reduce publication bias.
- Explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, with screening and data extraction done independently by two reviewers.
- Assessment of each study's risk of bias (e.g. with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials).
- Synthesis: narrative, or statistical (meta-analysis) if studies are similar enough.
- Reporting guided by the PRISMA statement (first published 2009, updated in 2020).

Meta-analysis
- Statistically combines results from several studies to give a pooled estimate with greater precision.
- Studies are weighted, usually by the inverse of their variance, so larger and more precise studies count for more.
- Fixed-effect model: assumes one true effect shared by all studies. Random-effects model: assumes true effects vary between studies; gives wider CIs when studies disagree.

Reading a forest plot
- Each study is a square (its point estimate; the size of the square reflects its weight) with a horizontal line (its CI).
- The diamond at the bottom is the pooled estimate; its width is the pooled CI.
- The vertical line is the line of no effect: 1 for ratios (OR, RR), 0 for differences.
- If the diamond does not touch the line of no effect, the pooled result is statistically significant.
- The Cochrane Collaboration's logo is a forest plot of trials of antenatal corticosteroids for women at risk of preterm birth, showing how pooling revealed a benefit individual trials had missed.

Heterogeneity
- Variation between study results beyond what chance would produce. Assessed visually (do the CIs overlap?) and statistically (Cochran's Q test; the I² statistic, the percentage of variation due to heterogeneity rather than chance; roughly, 25%, 50% and 75% are often described as low, moderate and high).
- Substantial heterogeneity should prompt a search for its causes (different populations, doses, designs) and caution about pooling.

Publication bias
- Studies with positive or striking results are more likely to be published, published faster and published in English, so a review of published studies may overestimate benefit.
- Detected using a funnel plot (study effect against its precision): asymmetry, such as missing small negative studies, suggests publication bias, although asymmetry has other causes.
- Prevented by prospective trial registration and searching registers and grey literature.

From evidence to practice
- The GRADE approach rates the certainty of a body of evidence (high, moderate, low, very low) and the strength of recommendations.
- Guidelines (e.g. from NICE in England) translate this evidence into recommendations; clinicians still need to apply them to individual patients.

Exam tips: be able to read every element of a forest plot and say whether the pooled result is significant, and know what a funnel plot is for.

Diagnostic tests are judged by comparing them with a reference ("gold") standard. Lay results out in a 2×2 table: columns show true disease status, rows show test result.

- True positives (TP): a; false positives (FP): b
- False negatives (FN): c; true negatives (TN): d

Measures
- Sensitivity = a/(a + c): the proportion of people with the disease who test positive.
- Specificity = d/(b + d): the proportion of people without the disease who test negative.
- Positive predictive value PPV = a/(a + b): the probability that someone who tests positive has the disease.
- Negative predictive value NPV = d/(c + d): the probability that someone who tests negative is disease-free.
- Mnemonics: SnNout (a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules out) and SpPin (a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules in).

The key point: predictive values depend on prevalence
Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test (though they can vary between settings). PPV and NPV change with how common the disease is in the people tested.

Worked example: 10,000 people, prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%.
- 100 have the disease: 90 TP, 10 FN.
- 9,900 do not: 95% of them (9,405) are TN, so 495 are FP.
- PPV = 90/(90 + 495) = 90/585 ≈ 15%.
- NPV = 9,405/(9,405 + 10) ≈ 99.9%.
So even with a good test, most positives in a low-prevalence population are false positives. The same test in a high-prevalence clinic would have a much higher PPV.

Likelihood ratios
- LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity.
- In the example, LR+ = 0.90/0.05 = 18 and LR− = 0.10/0.95 ≈ 0.11. Large LR+ values (e.g. above 10) and small LR− values (e.g. below 0.1) shift the probability of disease substantially.
- Moving a test's cut-off trades sensitivity against specificity; a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots sensitivity against 1 − specificity across cut-offs.

Screening
Screening means testing apparently healthy people to find disease or risk factors early, so that earlier action improves outcomes. In the UK, the UK National Screening Committee advises on which programmes to offer.

The Wilson and Jungner principles (WHO, 1968) include:
- the condition is an important health problem
- there is an accepted treatment, and facilities for diagnosis and treatment are available
- there is a recognisable latent or early symptomatic stage
- there is a suitable, acceptable test
- the natural history is adequately understood
- there is an agreed policy on whom to treat
- the cost is balanced against overall spending on care
- case-finding is a continuing process, not a one-off

Potential benefits: earlier diagnosis, less radical treatment, lives saved, reassurance for true negatives.
Potential harms: false positives (anxiety, further invasive tests), false negatives (false reassurance), overdiagnosis (detecting disease that would never have caused harm) and overtreatment, and costs.

Biases that make screening look better than it is
- Lead-time bias: diagnosis is earlier, so survival from diagnosis looks longer even if death occurs at the same time.
- Length-time bias: slow-growing, less aggressive disease spends longer in the detectable phase and is more likely to be picked up.
- Volunteer (selection) bias: people who attend screening tend to be healthier.
The fair test is an RCT of screening versus no screening with disease-specific or all-cause mortality as the outcome.

Exam tips: always build the 2×2 table from the prevalence first, and explain why survival time from diagnosis is a misleading measure of screening benefit.

cards.b: The conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients, integrating research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values.
Population/patient, Intervention (or exposure), Comparison, Outcome: a framework for turning a clinical problem into a focused, searchable research question.
Ask a focused question, Acquire evidence, Appraise it, Apply it with expertise and patient preferences, Assess the outcome.

cards.f: Boolean OR vs AND in a literature search
cards.b: OR combines synonyms and widens a search (more results); AND combines different concepts (e.g. P and I) and narrows it (fewer results).

cards.f: Best design for a harm/aetiology question
cards.b: Cohort or case-control study, since deliberately randomising people to a harmful exposure would be unethical.
Medical Subject Headings: the controlled vocabulary used to index MEDLINE, so searches catch articles that use different words for the same concept.
A measure (e.g. a blood test or BP) used in place of a patient-important outcome (e.g. death, stroke). Improving a surrogate does not always improve the real outcome.
Starts with people with the outcome (cases) and without (controls) and compares past exposure. Good for rare diseases; prone to recall and selection bias; yields an odds ratio.
Classifies people free of the outcome by exposure and follows them to see who develops it. Establishes temporality and incidence; yields relative risk; slow and costly.
Measures exposure and outcome at one time point. Gives prevalence; cannot establish which came first.
Wrongly assuming that an association seen between groups (e.g. countries) also holds for the individuals within them.
Keeping the next random allocation hidden from those enrolling participants, so they cannot influence who goes into which group (prevents selection bias).

Analysing participants in the groups to which they were randomised, whatever treatment they actually received. Preserves randomisation; usually a conservative estimate of benefit in superiority trials.
Randomisation (in a large enough trial) balances known and unknown confounders between groups, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the intervention.
Internal: results are correct for the study participants (free of bias/confounding). External: results can be generalised to other people and settings.
Dividing the population into subgroups (e.g. age bands) and randomly sampling within each, so each subgroup is represented.
Both categorical. Nominal categories have no order (blood group); ordinal categories have a natural order (cancer stage, pain severity).
Median and interquartile range, because the mean and SD are distorted by the long tail.
Long tail to the right; mean is greater than median (e.g. length of hospital stay).
About 95% of values lie within 1.96 SD of the mean (about 68% within 1 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD).
SE = SD/√n. Measures the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean; falls as sample size increases.
Sampling error is random and shrinks with larger samples; bias is systematic and is not reduced by increasing sample size.
The probability of getting a result at least as extreme as that observed if the null hypothesis were true. Not the probability that the null is true.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive). Probability = α, usually 0.05.
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative). Probability = β.
1 − β: the probability of detecting a true effect of a given size. Increased by larger sample, bigger effect, less variability, or higher α.
Estimate ± 1.96 × SE.
0 for differences (in means or risks); 1 for ratios (RR, OR, HR). A 95% CI that excludes it corresponds to p < 0.05.
A result can be statistically significant but too small to matter to patients (common in huge studies), or clinically important but non-significant (small studies).
Compares means of two related measurements (e.g. before and after in the same people) by testing whether the mean difference is zero. Assumes differences are roughly Normal.
Independent observations, roughly Normal data in each group and (Student's version) similar variances.
Non-parametric test comparing two independent groups (also called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test). Used for skewed or ordinal data.
Non-parametric test for paired data or one sample; alternative to the paired t-test.
Compares proportions between independent groups in a contingency table; expected counts should mostly be at least 5. 2×2 table has 1 degree of freedom.
Used instead of chi-squared for a 2×2 table with small expected counts.
Tests paired binary data, e.g. the same patients classified by two different tests.
Pearson's r measures linear association between Normal numerical variables; Spearman's uses ranks and is non-parametric.
RR = [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)]: risk in exposed divided by risk in unexposed.
OR = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc.
ARR = control event rate − experimental event rate.
NNT = 1/ARR (rounded up): the number of patients treated for one extra to benefit.
RRR = ARR/CER = 1 − RR.
When the outcome is rare (roughly under 10%). For common outcomes, the OR lies further from 1 than the RR.
Participants are selected by outcome, so the investigator fixes the proportion with disease and risks cannot be calculated; the OR remains valid.
A variable associated with the exposure, independently associated with the outcome, and not on the causal pathway between them.
Cases remember or report past exposures differently from controls; a typical weakness of case-control studies.
Employed people are healthier than the general population, so comparing workers with the general public underestimates harms of an occupational exposure.
Design: randomisation, restriction, matching. Analysis: stratification, multivariable regression (adjustment).
The outcome causes the exposure rather than vice versa (e.g. illness leading people to stop drinking).
Strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy.

cards.f: The only essential Bradford Hill criterion
cards.b: Temporality: the cause must precede the effect.
The size of an effect genuinely differs between subgroups (e.g. by sex); a real finding to report, unlike confounding.
A review using a pre-specified, reproducible method to find, appraise and synthesise all relevant studies on a focused question.
Statistical pooling of results from several studies, weighted (usually by inverse variance), to give a more precise overall estimate.
The pooled estimate; its width is the pooled CI. If it does not cross the line of no effect, the pooled result is significant.
Percentage of variability between study results due to heterogeneity rather than chance; roughly 25%/50%/75% = low/moderate/high.
Plot of study effect size against precision; asymmetry (e.g. missing small negative studies) suggests publication bias.
Studies with positive results are more likely to be published, so reviews of published work may overestimate benefit.
Reporting guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (2009, updated 2020), including a flow diagram of study selection.
Fixed: assumes one true effect across studies. Random: assumes true effects vary; gives wider CIs when studies disagree.
TP/(TP + FN): proportion of people with the disease who test positive.
TN/(TN + FP): proportion of people without the disease who test negative.
TP/(TP + FP): probability that a person testing positive has the disease. Rises with prevalence.
A highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules out; a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules in.
LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity).
Screening diagnoses disease earlier, so survival from diagnosis appears longer even if the time of death is unchanged.
Screening preferentially detects slow-growing disease with a long detectable phase, which has a better prognosis anyway.
Detection of disease that would never have caused symptoms or death in the person's lifetime, leading to unnecessary treatment.

questions.q: A GP asks: 'In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does physiotherapy compared with no treatment reduce pain at 6 months?' In PICO terms, what is 'no treatment'?
questions.why: No treatment is what physiotherapy is compared against, so it is the comparison. Physiotherapy is the intervention, adults with knee osteoarthritis are the population and pain at 6 months is the outcome.

questions.q: Which study design is usually most appropriate for asking whether a common drug increases the risk of a rare birth defect?
options: A cross-sectional survey of pregnant women
questions.why: A rare outcome and a possibly harmful exposure point to a case-control study: start with affected babies and controls and compare drug exposure. Randomising pregnant women to a suspected teratogen would be unethical; a cross-sectional survey cannot establish timing and would find few cases; a case report has no comparison group.

questions.q: Define evidence-based practice and explain why it is not the same as simply following the results of trials.
markScheme: Accurate definition (e.g. Sackett 1996: conscientious, explicit, judicious use of current best evidence in decisions about individual patients)
Identifies the three components: best research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values/preferences
Explains that trials give average effects in selected populations, so applicability to the individual must be judged
Notes patient preferences and circumstances may lead to a different decision from the 'average' best option
questions.modelAnswer: Evidence-based practice is the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about individual patients (Sackett and colleagues, 1996). It combines three things: the best available research, the clinician's expertise and the patient's values and circumstances. It is not the same as following trial results mechanically. Trials report average effects in selected participants who may differ from the patient in age, other illnesses or other medicines, so the clinician must judge whether the evidence applies. And a patient who weighs benefits and harms differently, for example preferring to avoid daily medication, may reasonably choose a different option. Expertise and patient values are therefore part of EBP, not exceptions to it.

questions.q: Researchers identify 300 patients with mesothelioma and 600 without, then ask both groups about past asbestos exposure. What design is this?
questions.why: Participants are selected by outcome (mesothelioma or not) and past exposure is compared, which defines a case-control study. A cohort study would select by exposure and follow people forward; there is no allocated intervention, so it is not a trial; and a cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at one time point without selecting on disease status.

questions.q: In an RCT, 15% of patients randomised to the new drug stopped taking it. Which analysis best preserves the benefits of randomisation?
options: Analysing only patients who completed the trial
Re-assigning non-adherent patients to the control group
questions.why: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone in the group to which they were randomised, keeping groups comparable. Per-protocol analysis, analysing completers only, and moving non-adherent patients to the control group all break randomisation, because those who stop treatment may differ systematically (e.g. sicker) from those who continue.

questions.q: Compare cohort and case-control studies, giving two strengths and one weakness of each.
markScheme: Cohort: selected by exposure, followed forward for outcome; case-control: selected by outcome, look back at exposure
Cohort strengths: establishes temporality; measures incidence/RR; good for rare exposures or several outcomes
Cohort weakness: slow, costly, loss to follow-up, inefficient for rare outcomes
Case-control strengths: quick, cheap, good for rare diseases or long latency, many exposures
Case-control weakness: recall bias, control selection bias, cannot give incidence (OR only)
questions.modelAnswer: A cohort study selects people free of the outcome, classifies them by exposure and follows them to see who develops the outcome. It establishes that exposure came before outcome and measures incidence, so it gives relative risks; it suits rare exposures and can study several outcomes. However it is slow and expensive, loses participants to follow-up and is inefficient for rare outcomes. A case-control study starts with people who have the outcome and matched or comparable controls and looks back at their past exposure. It is quick and cheap and is the design of choice for rare diseases or those with long latency, and many exposures can be examined. Its weaknesses are recall bias (cases may remember exposures differently), difficulty choosing appropriate controls, and the fact that incidence cannot be calculated, so only odds ratios are available.

questions.q: Length of hospital stay in a sample is strongly right-skewed. Which summary is most appropriate?
questions.why: For skewed data the median and IQR describe a typical value and spread without being distorted by the long tail. The mean and SD are pulled by extreme values; the standard error describes precision of a mean, not spread; the mode and range are unstable and the range depends entirely on the two extremes.

questions.q: A study's sample size is increased from 100 to 400, with the same SD. What happens to the standard error of the mean?
questions.why: SE = SD/√n. Multiplying n by 4 multiplies √n by 2, so the SE halves. Quartering would need n to rise 16-fold; the SE cannot rise as n increases; and it would only stay the same if n did not change.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the standard deviation and the standard error of the mean, and say when each should be reported.
markScheme: SD describes variability of individual observations around the mean
SE = SD/√n describes the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean
SE shrinks as n increases; SD does not systematically change with n
Report SD to describe the data; use SE (or better, a CI) when making inferences about the population mean
questions.modelAnswer: The standard deviation measures how spread out individual observations are around the mean, for example how much systolic pressure varies between patients. The standard error of the mean equals SD/√n and measures how precisely the sample mean estimates the true population mean. Increasing the sample size reduces the SE, because the mean becomes more precise, but does not systematically change the SD, which reflects real variation between people. The SD should be used to describe the sample (mean ± SD for Normal data), while the SE is used for inference, usually by converting it into a confidence interval (mean ± 1.96 SE). Reporting SE in place of SD makes data look less variable than they are.

questions.q: A trial reports p = 0.03 for the difference between drug and placebo. Which statement is correct?
options: If there were truly no difference, a result at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 97% probability that the drug works
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
The drug's effect is large enough to be clinically important
questions.why: The p value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true: it is the probability of data at least as extreme as those observed under that assumption. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true or that the drug works, and it says nothing about the size or clinical importance of the effect.

questions.q: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.85 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.03). What can you conclude?
options: The result is not statistically significant at the 5% level
The study must have been perfectly powered
The drug significantly reduces risk by 15%
questions.why: For a ratio, the line of no effect is 1. The interval runs from 0.70 to 1.03, so it includes 1 and p > 0.05. The point estimate suggests a 15% reduction, but this is not statistically significant; nothing indicates increased risk; and a wide CI crossing 1 suggests the study may have been underpowered rather than perfectly powered.

questions.q: A trial finds a mean reduction in HbA1c of 4 mmol/mol with a new drug compared with placebo, standard error 1.5 mmol/mol. Calculate the 95% confidence interval, interpret it, and explain what is meant by a type II error.
markScheme: CI ≈ 1.06 to 6.94 mmol/mol
Excludes 0, so statistically significant at 5% level; true effect plausibly between about 1 and 7 mmol/mol
Clinical importance depends on whether values in the CI are meaningful to patients
Type II error: failing to detect a real effect (false negative), probability β; power = 1 − β
questions.modelAnswer: The 95% CI is 4 ± 1.96 × 1.5 = 4 ± 2.94, giving 1.06 to 6.94 mmol/mol. Because the interval does not include 0 (the line of no effect for a difference), the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. The true average effect is plausibly anywhere from about 1 to 7 mmol/mol; whether this matters clinically depends on whether the lower end of that range would be worthwhile for patients. A type II error is failing to reject the null hypothesis when there really is an effect, a false negative. Its probability is β, and power (1 − β) is the chance of detecting a true effect of a given size; small trials have low power and a higher risk of type II error.

questions.q: Peak expiratory flow is measured in 30 asthmatic patients before and after an inhaler. The differences are approximately Normally distributed. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.why: The same patients are measured twice, so the data are paired, and the differences are Normal, so a paired t-test fits. An independent t-test and the Mann–Whitney U test treat the groups as separate people, and the chi-squared test is for categorical outcomes, not continuous measurements.

questions.q: Two independent groups are compared on a pain score that is ordinal (0–10) and strongly skewed. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.why: Skewed or ordinal data from two independent groups call for the Mann–Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test. The paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test are for paired data, and Pearson correlation measures linear association between two numerical variables rather than comparing groups.

questions.q: In a trial, 30 of 100 treated patients and 50 of 100 control patients are readmitted. Calculate the chi-squared statistic and state your conclusion (the 5% critical value for 1 degree of freedom is 3.84).
markScheme: Expected readmissions per arm = 100 × 80/200 = 40; expected non-readmissions = 60
8.33 > 3.84, so p < 0.05: reject null hypothesis; readmission rates differ
States assumptions: independent groups, expected counts ≥ 5
questions.modelAnswer: Overall 80 of 200 patients are readmitted. Under the null hypothesis, expected counts in each arm are 100 × 80/200 = 40 readmitted and 60 not readmitted. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = (30 − 40)²/40 + (70 − 60)²/60 + (50 − 40)²/40 + (50 − 60)²/60 = 2.5 + 1.67 + 2.5 + 1.67 ≈ 8.33. With 1 degree of freedom, 8.33 exceeds the critical value of 3.84, so p < 0.05 and we reject the null hypothesis: the treated group had a significantly lower readmission rate (30% vs 50%). The test is valid because the groups are independent and all expected counts are well above 5.

questions.q: In an RCT, the event rate is 8% in the control group and 6% in the treatment group. What is the number needed to treat?
questions.why: ARR = 8% − 6% = 2% = 0.02, so NNT = 1/0.02 = 50. 2 is the ARR expressed as a percentage, not its reciprocal; 25 is the relative risk reduction as a percentage (0.02/0.08 = 25%), not an NNT; and 4 is 1/RRR (1/0.25), the slip of taking the reciprocal of the relative rather than the absolute risk reduction.

questions.q: A case-control study of a common outcome reports an odds ratio of 3.0. Why might this overstate the relative risk?
options: Case-control studies always overestimate associations because of confounding
When an outcome is common, the odds ratio lies further from 1 than the relative risk
The odds ratio equals the relative risk squared
The odds ratio is calculated from incidence, which is inflated in case-control studies
questions.why: The OR approximates the RR only when the outcome is rare; for common outcomes it is further from 1, so an OR of 3 overstates the RR. Confounding can bias any observational design in either direction, not always upwards; case-control studies cannot measure incidence at all; and there is no fixed squared relationship between OR and RR.

questions.q: In a cohort of 1,000 smokers, 40 develop COPD over 10 years; in 2,000 non-smokers, 20 develop COPD. Construct the 2×2 table and calculate the risk in each group, the relative risk, the odds ratio and the attributable (excess) risk. Interpret the RR.
markScheme: Table: smokers 40 COPD / 960 no COPD; non-smokers 20 / 1,980
Risk smokers = 40/1,000 = 4%; non-smokers = 20/2,000 = 1%
Attributable risk = 4% − 1% = 3% (30 per 1,000 over 10 years)
Interpretation: smokers have 4 times the 10-year risk; OR close to RR because outcome is uncommon
questions.modelAnswer: Table: smokers 40 with COPD and 960 without; non-smokers 20 with COPD and 1,980 without. Risk in smokers = 40/1,000 = 0.04 (4%); risk in non-smokers = 20/2,000 = 0.01 (1%). RR = 0.04/0.01 = 4. OR = (40 × 1,980)/(960 × 20) = 79,200/19,200 = 4.125. Attributable risk = 0.04 − 0.01 = 0.03, i.e. 30 extra cases per 1,000 smokers over 10 years, if the association is causal. Smokers had four times the 10-year risk of developing COPD compared with non-smokers. The OR is close to the RR because COPD is fairly uncommon in this cohort; confounding (e.g. occupational dust exposure) would need to be considered before attributing all the excess to smoking.

questions.q: An observational study finds that people who carry lighters have higher rates of lung cancer. What best explains this?
questions.why: Smoking is associated with carrying a lighter and independently causes lung cancer, and it is not on a causal pathway from lighters to cancer, so it is a classic confounder. Recall bias concerns differential reporting of past exposures; reverse causation would mean lung cancer makes people carry lighters; lead-time bias relates to screening and survival time.

questions.q: Which method controls for both known and unknown confounders?
questions.why: Randomisation in a large enough trial balances all confounders, measured or not, between groups. Matching, multivariable adjustment and restriction can deal only with confounders that were identified and measured.

questions.q: Define confounding, give an example, and describe two ways it can be controlled at the design stage and one at the analysis stage.
markScheme: Definition: third variable associated with exposure and independently with outcome, not on causal pathway
Valid example (e.g. smoking confounding coffee–lung cancer; age confounding grey hair–mortality)
Design: randomisation (balances known and unknown confounders)
Design: restriction or matching
Analysis: stratification (e.g. Mantel–Haenszel) or multivariable regression; note residual confounding
questions.modelAnswer: Confounding occurs when a third variable is associated with the exposure, is independently associated with the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway between them, so it creates or distorts an apparent association. For example, coffee drinkers appear to have more lung cancer because coffee drinkers are more likely to smoke, and smoking causes lung cancer. At the design stage, randomisation balances known and unknown confounders between groups; alternatively, restriction (e.g. studying only non-smokers) or matching cases and controls on the confounder removes its influence. At the analysis stage, results can be stratified by the confounder or adjusted using multivariable regression. Analytical adjustment only deals with measured confounders, so residual confounding remains possible in observational studies.

questions.q: On a forest plot of odds ratios, the pooled diamond lies entirely to the left of the vertical line at 1, where left favours treatment. What does this mean?
options: There is evidence of publication bias
The pooled result shows a statistically significant benefit of treatment
There is no significant difference between treatment and control
questions.why: If the diamond (pooled estimate and CI) does not cross the line of no effect, the pooled effect is statistically significant, here favouring treatment. A diamond crossing 1 would mean no significant difference; heterogeneity is judged from the spread of individual studies and I²; publication bias is assessed with a funnel plot, not the diamond.

questions.q: A funnel plot of 20 trials shows that small trials with negative results are missing from one side. What does this most likely suggest?
questions.why: Asymmetry with missing small negative studies is the classic sign of publication bias (though other causes of asymmetry exist). Confounding concerns third variables within studies; heterogeneity is about variation between study results, not a missing corner; lead-time bias relates to screening.

questions.q: Describe the main steps in carrying out a systematic review and explain how reviewers try to minimise publication bias.
markScheme: Focused question (e.g. PICO) and pre-registered protocol (e.g. PROSPERO)
Comprehensive search of multiple databases plus trial registers/grey literature
Explicit inclusion criteria, independent screening and data extraction by two reviewers
Risk-of-bias assessment and synthesis (narrative or meta-analysis), reported per PRISMA
Publication bias minimised by searching registers/unpublished data and assessed with funnel plots
questions.modelAnswer: A systematic review starts with a focused question, often framed as PICO, and a written protocol registered in advance (for example on PROSPERO) so methods cannot be changed after results are seen. Reviewers then search several databases such as MEDLINE, Embase and the Cochrane Library, plus trial registers, reference lists and grey literature. Studies are screened against explicit inclusion criteria, and data are extracted, ideally independently by two reviewers. Each study's risk of bias is assessed, and the results are synthesised narratively or, if studies are similar enough, by meta-analysis, with reporting following PRISMA. Publication bias is reduced by looking beyond published journals (trial registers, conference abstracts, contacting authors, no language restrictions) and is assessed with funnel plots, where asymmetry suggests missing small negative studies.

questions.q: A test has sensitivity 80% and specificity 90%. It is used in 1,000 people in whom prevalence is 10%. What is the positive predictive value?
questions.why: 100 have the disease: 80 test positive. 900 do not: 10% of them (90) test falsely positive. PPV = 80/(80 + 90) ≈ 47%. 80% is the sensitivity and 90% the specificity, not predictive values; about 97% is close to the NPV (810/830).

questions.q: A screening programme shows that 5-year survival from diagnosis is longer in screen-detected cancers, but death rates from the cancer are unchanged. Which bias best explains this?
questions.why: Earlier diagnosis moves the start of the survival clock forward, so survival from diagnosis lengthens without any delay in death: lead-time bias. Recall bias affects reports of past exposure, confounding by indication concerns treatment choice in observational studies, and observer bias involves assessors' knowledge of group allocation.

questions.q: Using the Wilson and Jungner principles, outline four criteria a condition and test should meet before a screening programme is introduced, and describe two harms of screening.
markScheme: Condition is an important health problem with understood natural history
Recognisable latent/early stage and accepted, effective treatment with facilities available
Suitable, acceptable test; agreed policy on whom to treat; cost balanced; continuous process (any four)
Harm: false positives causing anxiety and invasive follow-up
Harm: overdiagnosis/overtreatment or false reassurance from false negatives
questions.modelAnswer: Wilson and Jungner (WHO, 1968) set out principles including: the condition should be an important health problem; its natural history should be adequately understood, with a recognisable latent or early symptomatic stage; there should be an accepted, effective treatment and facilities for diagnosis and treatment; and there should be a suitable test that is acceptable to the population. Others include an agreed policy on whom to treat, costs balanced against overall spending, and case-finding as a continuing process. Harms include false positives, which cause anxiety and lead to unnecessary invasive tests such as biopsies, and overdiagnosis, where disease that would never have caused harm is found and treated, exposing people to side effects without benefit. False negatives can also give false reassurance and delay diagnosis of symptoms later.

questions.q:
A randomised trial compares a new anticoagulant with standard treatment for preventing stroke in atrial fibrillation. Of 2,000 patients on the new drug, 60 have a stroke; of 2,000 on standard treatment, 90 have a stroke. Major bleeding occurs in 50 patients on the new drug and 30 on standard treatment.
(a) Calculate the relative risk, relative risk reduction, absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat for stroke. (8 marks)
(b) Calculate the number needed to harm for major bleeding. (3 marks)
(c) The paper reports RR for stroke 0.67 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.92). Interpret this. (3 marks)
(d) Discuss how you would use these results with an individual patient, and two features of the trial design you would check before trusting them. (6 marks)
markScheme: (a) Stroke risk: new 60/2,000 = 3%; standard 90/2,000 = 4.5%
(b) Bleeding: 2.5% vs 1.5%, absolute risk increase 1% (0.01), NNH = 100
(c) CI excludes 1 so significant at 5% level; true reduction plausibly from 8% to 52%
(d) Weigh benefit (1 stroke prevented per 67) against harm (1 extra major bleed per 100) with patient's own baseline risk and values
(d) Design checks: randomisation and allocation concealment; blinding; intention-to-treat; loss to follow-up; generalisability of participants
Credit for noting absolute vs relative framing and that stroke and bleeding may differ in severity
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Stroke risk is 60/2,000 = 0.030 on the new drug and 90/2,000 = 0.045 on standard treatment. RR = 0.030/0.045 ≈ 0.67. RRR = 1 − 0.67 ≈ 33%. ARR = 0.045 − 0.030 = 0.015 (1.5 percentage points). NNT = 1/0.015 ≈ 66.7, rounded up to 67: about 67 patients must take the new drug instead of standard treatment for one extra stroke to be prevented over the trial period.

(b) Major bleeding is 50/2,000 = 2.5% on the new drug and 30/2,000 = 1.5% on standard treatment, an absolute risk increase of 1% (0.01). NNH = 1/0.01 = 100: for every 100 patients treated with the new drug, one extra major bleed occurs.

(c) The relative risk of 0.67 means a one-third reduction in stroke risk. The 95% CI (0.48 to 0.92) excludes 1, so the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. The true reduction could plausibly be as large as 52% or as small as 8%, so there is some uncertainty about its size.

(d) For an individual, I would explain absolute as well as relative effects: per 100 patients over the trial period, about 1.5 fewer strokes but about 1 more major bleed. A patient's own baseline stroke risk (e.g. from a risk score) and bleeding risk change the balance: someone at higher stroke risk gains more in absolute terms. Strokes are often more disabling than many bleeds, but the patient's own values, other medicines and practical issues such as monitoring matter. Before trusting the results I would check internal validity: was randomisation properly done with allocation concealment; were patients and outcome assessors blinded; was the analysis by intention to treat; and was loss to follow-up small and similar between arms. I would also check external validity: whether the participants (age, kidney function, comorbidities) resemble my patient, and who funded the trial.

questions.q:
A new blood test for colorectal cancer has sensitivity 85% and specificity 92%. It is proposed for population screening of adults aged 50–74, in whom the prevalence of undetected colorectal cancer is about 0.5%.
(a) For 100,000 people screened, construct a 2×2 table and calculate the PPV and NPV. (8 marks)
(b) Explain why the PPV in a symptomatic clinic population would differ. (3 marks)
(c) Discuss whether this test should be introduced as a screening programme, referring to established screening criteria and to biases in evaluating screening. (9 marks)
markScheme: (a) 500 with cancer: TP = 425, FN = 75; 99,500 without: TN = 91,540, FP = 7,960
(b) PPV rises with prevalence; symptomatic patients have higher pre-test probability, so fewer false positives per true positive
(c) Wilson and Jungner: important condition, early stage, effective treatment, acceptable test, agreed policy, cost, capacity for follow-up colonoscopy
(c) Harms: ~8,000 false positives needing colonoscopy (risks, anxiety, cost); missed cancers; overdiagnosis
(c) Lead-time, length-time and volunteer bias: need RCT evidence of reduced colorectal (and ideally all-cause) mortality
(c) Balanced conclusion, e.g. compare with existing programme and decision by UK National Screening Committee
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Of 100,000 people, 0.5% (500) have cancer and 99,500 do not. True positives = 85% of 500 = 425; false negatives = 75. True negatives = 92% of 99,500 = 91,540; false positives = 99,500 − 91,540 = 7,960. Total positives = 425 + 7,960 = 8,385, so PPV = 425/8,385 ≈ 5.1%. Total negatives = 91,540 + 75 = 91,615, so NPV = 91,540/91,615 ≈ 99.9%.

(b) Predictive values depend on prevalence. In a clinic of people with symptoms such as rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habit, the pre-test probability is much higher, so the same false-positive rate produces far fewer false positives per true positive and the PPV rises. Sensitivity and specificity may also differ, because symptomatic cancers tend to be more advanced.

(c) Colorectal cancer meets several Wilson and Jungner principles: it is an important health problem, it has a recognisable precancerous and early stage, and early-stage disease has effective treatment. But the test itself raises problems. About 19 out of every 20 positives are false (PPV about 5%), so around 8,000 people per 100,000 screened would need colonoscopy, with its discomfort, small risks of perforation and bleeding, anxiety and cost, and there must be enough colonoscopy capacity. 75 cancers would be missed, and negative results might falsely reassure people who later develop symptoms. Overdiagnosis is possible if small lesions that would never progress are found. Acceptability matters: a blood test might raise uptake compared with stool tests, which could be a real advantage. Evaluating benefit is difficult because of lead-time bias (survival from diagnosis lengthens even if death is not delayed), length-time bias (slow-growing tumours are preferentially found) and volunteer bias (attenders are healthier). So the key evidence should come from randomised trials showing reduced colorectal cancer mortality, ideally without increased all-cause mortality, and comparison with the existing screening test. In the UK such a decision would be made by the UK National Screening Committee. On these figures the test should not replace existing screening until trial evidence shows a mortality benefit that outweighs the burden of false positives.
